tip: A future time phrase with no preposition normally takes the accusative: 'nächsten Sommer' = next summer.
'Herr' adds '-n' in every singular case except the nominative: 'ich suche Herrn Schmidt'.
'Euro' stays singular after a number: 'zweihundert Euro', never 'Euros'.
'Helfen' takes the dative, not the accusative: 'sie hilft ihren Eltern' = she helps her parents.
Yes-no questions start with the verb: 'haben Sie eine Reservierung' = do you have a reservation.
The suffix '-bar' builds adjectives from verbs: 'dankbar' = grateful, from 'danken' = to thank.
'Schreiben an' plus the accusative means to write to: 'an meine Oma' = to my grandma.
Accusative masculine: after 'einen' the adjective ends in '-en'. So 'einen guten Tag', not 'einen gut Tag'.
'Obst', meaning fruit, stays singular with no plural: 'frisches Obst'.
After 'ich glaube' you can drop 'dass'; then the word order stays normal: 'das ist eine gute Idee'.
'Von' plus the dative expresses of: 'der Geruch von frischem Brot' = the smell of fresh bread.
Clock times use 'um', often on a 24-hour clock: 'um vierzehn Uhr' = at 14:00, i.e. 2 pm.
'Hätte gern' is a polite way to order: 'ich hätte gern einen Kaffee' = I would like a coffee.
German has hunger rather than being hungry: 'ich habe Hunger' is literally I have hunger.
'Nach' takes the dative: 'nach einem neuen Mitarbeiter' uses 'einem', not 'einen'.
With 'seit', German stays in the present: 'lerne seit einem Jahr' = have been learning for a year.
'Seit' plus the present covers since or for an ongoing situation: 'seit gestern' = since yesterday.
'Gern' after a verb means like to: 'erzählt gern Geschichten' = likes to tell stories.
Nouns built with the ending '-ung' are feminine: 'die Heizung' = the heating.
'Nach' shows direction toward cities and most countries, with no article: 'nach München'.
'Angenehm!' is short for 'angenehm, Sie kennenzulernen' – a formal greeting.
After 'konnte', the remaining verb parts go to the very end: 'konnte ... zugestellt werden' = could be delivered.
German usually negates a noun with 'kein', not 'nicht': no more room = 'keinen Platz mehr'.
'Seit' with the present tense covers English has been doing: 'wartet schon seit einer Stunde' = has been waiting for an hour.
The verb stays second: after the opening time phrase 'um drei Uhr nachmittags', 'gibt' comes right away.
'Vorlesen' splits: the 'vor' breaks off to the very end, so 'liest' and 'vor' wrap the whole sentence.
'Für' always takes the accusative, which is why it is 'für den gesamten Nahverkehr', 'den' and not 'der'.
'Ausgiebig frühstücken' means having a long, generous breakfast, a classic German Sunday tradition.
Compounds take the gender of their last word, so every '-zimmer' word is neuter: 'das Wohnzimmer'.
Start with a time phrase and the verb still comes second, before the subject: 'heute Nachmittag holt mein Vater', not 'mein Vater holt'.
